On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram is still the palace guard under Basanta Ray’s command and the one who stands between Udayaditya and freedom; Udayaditya must force his way past him, and Sitaram is willing to be disarmed and bound rather than draw a weapon against the prince because the prince had saved his life twice. By the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, the roles are reversed: Sitaram becomes the agent of his rescue, entering the prison as his helper, telling him the prison is on fire, seizing him, and carrying him out; the guard who once hindered him becomes the man who frees him.

Pratapaditya’s first plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he stopped at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore. That attempt failed because the Pathans would not carry it out; one of them warned Basanta Ray and Udayaditya instead. The method that finally succeeded was a direct execution ordered by Pratapaditya: Muktiyar Khan carried out the command, and Abdul killed Basanta Ray with a drawn sword in the fort while the old king was praying.

In the palace inner quarters, disguised as Mother Nikasha, after mocking the court women and the Mahishi, and again in the king’s room, after insulting the princess of Jessore, Rammohan seizes Ramai by the scruff and throws him out.
A covert poisoning plot—Mangala preparing poison at the Rajmahishi’s behest, which Surma ingested and died from, making it seem like a self-inflicted death—was what actually caused her departure.
Her refusal led to the Maharaj marrying another woman, leaving Vibha with no place and no home in her own husband’s kingdom.

Rukmini took Udayaditya’s signet ring after he gave it to her in the confrontation, and that ring bore the Yubaraj’s seal. Bhagavat and Sitaram used that seal to forge a petition in the Yubaraj’s name accusing Pratapaditya of treason, then Bhagavat brought the forged document to Pratapaditya as if it had been carried by Udayaditya’s servant. Because the seal looked genuine, Pratapaditya accepted it as evidence and ordered Udayaditya imprisoned.

The escape’s aftermath made Pratapaditya suddenly pay special attention to Udayaditya and the inner quarters; because of that new scrutiny, he learned of the secret stipends Surma had arranged for Sitaram and Bhagavat through her maid. Seeing this as a direct defiance of his will, he became furious and ordered Surma to be sent away from the palace, which led to the decree exiling her.

The song carries the emotion of utter loneliness: a man who has lost the people and joys that made life meaningful, so that what remains is emptiness, unanswered calls, and the unbearable question of how to live on. Basanta Ray sings it in two sharply different moods. First, in Raigarh at sunset, alone on the veranda, the song rises as a private, melancholy lament for the vanished ones and the lost joy of earlier days. Second, in Jessore, when he stands before the silent, empty room where the household’s warmth has vanished and hears, “Those who were here before are here no more!” he sings it as a heart-rending cry of desolation before Vibha.

Because Rukmini failed to halt the midnight escape, Udayaditya got away with Basanta Ray, and when she later told Pratapaditya that “your Yubaraj escaped last night with the old king,” the king concluded Basanta Ray was responsible and issued the order for his execution; when Udayaditya was captured, that order was carried out and Basanta Ray was killed.

Pratapaditya’s first reception of Ramchandra was cool, almost dismissive: no elaborate welcome, no show of haste or respect, and he treated him as a lesser guest, sending him on to the inner quarters while continuing his own business; later, Ramchandra exacted the same sort of status display in his own court, turning it into a daily ritual of insult and mockery against Pratapaditya, insisting on his own superiority and humiliating Pratapaditya’s lineage and standing before everyone.

Rukmini, the widow from Raigarh, re-enters Udayaditya’s life as Mangala, a widow living on the outskirts of Jessore; there she wins the confidence of the palace servants, learns of Surma’s fate, and prepares the poison that brings about Surma’s death. Later, in a stormy night, she appears in Udayaditya’s bedchamber, accuses him of ruining her, and demands his ring, reawakening the past shame and guilt that turns his grief into tragedy.

His early lament—that as the crown prince he is trapped by a burden he cannot bear and is unfit to rule—deepens into a final conviction that his very existence has brought ruin to others. When confronted by Pratapaditya, he declares he is not worthy of the kingdom, asks to be released from the throne, and formally swears before Ma-Kali that he will never accept even an iota of Jessore, naming Samaraditya as heir and renouncing the throne for life.

Ramchandra Ray’s letter, written in anger to Pratapaditya renouncing Vibha, was not delivered to Jessore as intended. Nayanchand, who carried it, feared what might happen if Pratapaditya saw it, so he gave it to the Mahishi instead. The Mahishi hid the true contents and then deliberately misrepresented it to the household and to Vibha: she announced that Ramchandra Ray had written asking that Vibha be sent to her in-laws’ house. Convinced by this false account, Vibha believed her husband had forgiven her and wished to take her back, and her heart filled with joy.

Pratapaditya traps him by locking all exits and blocking the palace canal with sal logs, expecting the boat to be stranded. But Udayaditya opens the locked gate and Rammohan uses the palace roof above the canal to lower Ramchandra into the boat by rope; once there, they haul the boat over the logs and escape. The local pursuit fails because the guards waste precious time searching for a gun and then fetching another boat, and by the time they get it, the boat has already slipped away.

Basanta Ray’s sitar becomes a symbol of his shattered joy: it was once his “eternal companion,” but when he learns of Udayaditya’s imprisonment, he says the sitar is still there yet its strings are broken and cannot be tuned. That mirrors his despair—his music, hope, and reason to live have gone silent, leaving him to sing, “I alone am left behind,” and, at the end, to leave the sitar behind forever because the loss of Udayaditya has broken the heart that used to make it sing.

Earlier, Udayaditya had a reputation for bold, compassionate intervention: he would openly protect the oppressed and oppose injustice even when it meant risking himself. After Surma’s death, however, that willingness disappears; he becomes so overwhelmed by fear of Pratapaditya that he hesitates, refuses to help, and even withdraws from the suffering of the subjects, no longer daring to stand against their oppressors.

Sitaram undoes it by helping Basanta Ray rescue Udayaditya from the prison: he brings Basanta Ray there in secret, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and drags him out to safety, thereby reversing the false imprisonment he had helped Bhagavat engineer.

He does it in two desperate, physically daring escapes: first, he ties thick sheets into a rope from the palace roof to a boat in the canal below, then climbs down with Ramchandra on his back and lowers him into the boat; second, after defying the king, he lifts the unconscious Vibha out of the palace, places her in a waiting palanquin, and carries her to the boat to get her away.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed and displayed as a richly adorned bride—heavy gold bangles, a massive diamond bracelet, a large nose ring, elaborately styled hair, with her whole person burdened by ornaments and admired as if she belongs in a royal, festive court. By the time she seeks Ramchandra in Chandradwip, that whole presentation is inverted: she goes “dressed as a common woman,” refuses a palanquin and insists she will go “like a common subject, like a beggar-woman,” and when she reaches the palace she enters as an unwelcomed servant, with her veil fallen and her head bent in shame. The glittering, queenly image of the bride is replaced by a bare, humble, stripped-down appearance of a woman who has come in humiliation and desperation rather than pride.

After Surma’s death, the window in his bedchamber is the place of unbearable absence and longing: he keeps expecting Surma to be there, and it becomes a painful reminder that she is gone. In the prison, by contrast, the window becomes the place of hope and freedom: through its narrow opening he looks at the sky, sees the birds, and feels that his own cage may one day break and he may be released, so it symbolizes liberation, inner freedom, and the possibility of escape rather than grief.

At first, their connection is a money-lender/borrower parody of courtship: Sitaram, flat broke and full of swagger, keeps coming to Rukmini’s house for loans, flirting with pet names and teasing jokes while she treats the loan as business and he treats repayment as a joke. As his need grows, the flirtation hardens into conspiracy and then outright betrayal—he secretly plots around the Yubaraj’s imprisonment, helps set the prison fire, and, after the escape, thinks of Rukmini as a dead, money-bearing obstacle to steal from. But Rukmini has become consumed by grief, hatred, and the conviction that Sitaram and the Yubaraj are bound in her ruin; when he goes to her cottage to rob her, she is sitting in a ghostlike, soaked, rage-filled state and declares that she will burn him and the Yubaraj in the oven and kill him, then she rushes for a curved blade. Faced with that real, murderous fury instead of flirtation and interest, Sitaram’s swagger collapses into terror and flight.

At first, the fire is only a diversion: Sitaram uses the blaze to create panic in the palace and make the guards flee, leaving Udayaditya’s prison effectively unguarded so the escape can happen under cover of confusion. But once Udayaditya is out, the fire becomes a deliberate fraud. Sitaram and his men set the prison cell itself alight, scatter the evidence so it looks like a death in the flames, and plant bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword in the burning room. He then spreads the story that the Yubaraj died in the fire, manipulates the witnesses, and makes everyone believe the “death” story by the screams, the collapsed roof, the burnt sword fragments, and the rumor that reaches the king. He also destroys the letters that could have exposed the escape and flees before the truth can surface. In other words, what began as a simple smoke-and-chaos distraction mutates into a full cover-up: a staged prison fire, fabricated evidence, false testimony, and a calculated lie that the prince is dead, all designed to hide the fact that Udayaditya had escaped.

Ramchandra Ray later treats Udayaditya’s rescue as something done for his sister’s sake rather than as any act of loyalty or gratitude toward him, and in his own court he turns that into ridicule, mocking Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son instead of acknowledging the danger he had faced.

Because Bhagavat forged a petition in the Yubaraj’s name accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor of Delhi, Pratapaditya—who had mocked the Emperor as mere empty bluster—suddenly treated that imperial threat as real and used the alleged Delhi complaint as the pretext to imprison his son Udayaditya.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair functions as a daily sign of Surma’s loving presence: Surma is the one who usually comes to braid it, and Vibha waits for that familiar touch at the appointed hour. Once Surma is gone, the ritual becomes unbearable—Vibha sits quietly, expecting Surma to come, but evening falls and her hair remains unbraided, so the unfinished, uncombed hair becomes a visible marker of her tragic absence, a mute sign that the comfort, care, and companionship she once had in the palace are now lost forever.
